papers.title_in_file: A route to quantum computing through the theory of quantum graphs
papers.what_it_is: A pure-mathematics paper on graph C*-algebras and quantum graphs that proposes a (4n - 6)-qubit system built from Hamiltonian paths of a directed graph.

assertions.value: The paper states as Lemma 4.7, with a proof by induction on the degree recursion, that the number of distinct Hamiltonian paths in G(n) is 4n − 6.
quotes: Lemma 4.7. The number of distinct Hamiltonian paths in G(Πn) is equal to 4n − 6.
assertions.reader_inference: The proof checks small cases (n = 2 and 3) and a degree recurrence; it is a count on the authors' own graph family, not a statement about any quantum computer.

assertions.value: The authors claim, as Claim 4.20 and without proof, that the pre-assumed (4n − 6)-qubit quantum system for G(n) is not entangled.
quotes: Claim 4.20. In the case of G(Πn), the pre-assumed (4n − 6)-qubit quantum system is not entangled.
assertions.certainty_reason: Labelled a claim by the authors; its proof depends on a further claim from their earlier paper
assertions.reader_inference: The concluding remarks describe a 2-qubit entangled system, while Proposition 4.18 says the 2-qubit and 6-qubit systems are not entangled. The paper contradicts itself.

assertions.value: The authors claim, as Claim 4.23, that the quantum system arising from G(n) agrees and improves the ordinary classical systems.
quotes: Claim 4.23. The quantum system arising from G(Πn) agrees and improves (in quantum scale) the ordinary classical systems!
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated as a claim with no algorithm, experiment or proof in the paper
assertions.reader_inference: No task, algorithm or experiment is given, so the claim has no evidence in the paper.

papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Sections I to III, statements of Theorems 6, 7 and 9 with surrounding text, start of the noisy-circuit part of Section IV, Sections V and VI. Appendix proofs (continuity bounds) were not read.
papers.what_it_is: A theory paper that defines single-shot quantum classifiers and bounds how deterministic they can be, using quantum multi-hypothesis testing.

assertions.value: The authors define a quantum classifier as single-shot when the probability that a random output label equals the label assigned by majority vote is very high, independent of whether the labels are correct.
quotes: single-shot: exactly when the probability that a random label
assigned by the classifier is very high

assertions.value: The paper proves that how single-shot a quantum classifier can be is constrained by the distinguishability of the embedded quantum states, and that for circuit-based embeddings a certain depth is necessary for single-shotness to be possible.
assertions.anchor: Abstract; Theorems 6 and 9, Sections III and IV
quotes: show that the degree to which a quantum learning model is near-deterministic is constrained by the distinguishability of the embedded quantum states used in the model
a certain depth is necessary for single-shotness to be even possible
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorems 6 and 9, Sections III and IV (proofs in appendices, not read)
assertions.reader_inference: The depth bound is a necessary condition. The authors note the permitted error is not usually the error actually achieved by the circuit.

assertions.value: The authors argue that a learning model cannot be single-shot for all possible labelings of the input and also generalize, because such a model would be too expressive.
quotes: a learning model cannot be single-shot in a generic way, i.e. for all possible labelings of the input
it would become too expressive and there would be no meaningful way for such a model to generalize well
assertions.certainty_reason: Argument in Section V rests on a cited sample-complexity result (Ref. [6]) and a covering-number estimate, not on a stand-alone proof

assertions.value: The authors state that they only considered classification tasks and that extension to regression is left to future work.
quotes: First of all, we only considered classification tasks in this work.

papers.title_in_file: Data complexity signature predicts quantum projected learning benefit for antibiotic resistance
papers.what_it_is: An IBM and Cleveland Clinic empirical study of quantum projective learning on antibiotic resistance data, run in simulation and on IBM Eagle and Heron hardware.

assertions.value: The authors report that QPL did not consistently outperform classical baselines, that RF and XGB outperformed it for most antibiotics across 43,202 simulation experiments and 472 hardware experiments, and that it reached parity or better for nitrofurantoin and selected data splits.
quotes: While QPL did not consistently outperform classical baselines, potentially reflecting current quantum hardware limitations, it did achieve parity or superiority in specific scenarios, notably for the antibiotic nitrofurantoin and selected data splits
Across a total of 43,202 simulation-based experiments and 472 experiments based on hardware executions, we observed that RF and XGB outperformed QPL for the majority of antibiotics
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study on one dataset, Section 3.3
assertions.reader_inference: The attribution to hardware limits is the authors' speculation. Each split used 300 training and 75 test samples, so per-split differences are noisy.

assertions.value: The authors report that a logistic regression with elastic net penalty on data complexity measures separated QPL over- and under-performing hardware splits with an AUC of 0.88 and a p-value of 0.03, and that a similar model on all experiments gave no significant separation.
quotes: yielding an AUC of 0.88 and a p-value of 0.03
A similar regression model applied to all experiments, on both quantum hardware and simulator, did not yield a significant separation.
assertions.reader_inference: A p-value of 0.03 from a small number of splits, after selecting among 15 complexity measures with feature elimination, is weak evidence. The signature is not tested on new data.

assertions.value: The authors state that each antibiotic was evaluated on 10 coreset splits with 300 training and 75 test samples, and that the hardware experiments encoded over 60 input features.
quotes: we generated 10 coresets collections with each collection containing a 300 sample training set and 75 sample testing set.
The QPU experiments involved circuits encoding over 60 input features

assertions.value: The authors state that hardware constraints restricted exploration of larger feature spaces and more expressive circuits, limiting their ability to characterize scaling behavior.
quotes: Hardware constraints restricted exploration of larger feature spaces and more expressive circuits, limiting our ability to fully characterize scaling behavior.

papers.title_in_file: Escaping barren plateaus in approximate quantum compiling
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Sections 1, 2, parts of 3 and 4, Section 5 results text, Section 6. Appendices A and B (fast gradient, surrogate model) were not read.
papers.what_it_is: An IBM paper that proposes a classically computed local cost function to avoid barren plateaus when compiling quantum circuits and states.

assertions.value: The authors report that their truncated local cost functions can be calculated on a classical computer and are powerful enough to escape barren plateaus in approximate state preparation and full circuit approximation, significantly improving convergence.
quotes: we can significantly improve convergence with the approach developed in this work
can be feasibly calculated on a classical computer while also being powerful enough to escape barren plateaus that appear in both approximate state preparation and full circuit approximation
assertions.certainty_reason: Numerical simulations in Section 5, one ansatz and few targets
assertions.reader_inference: The compilation is classically simulated. The paper compares only against its own global cost function, not other compilers.

assertions.value: The authors show analytically, for a particular case, that coefficients exist such that the exponent in the gradient variance of the truncated cost function (equation 21) is increased by k relative to the global cost function.
quotes: such that the exponent that appears in the variance of the gradient of the truncated cost function in (21) is increased by k with respect to the global cost function
assertions.certainty_reason: Analytic derivation in Section 3 (equations 27 to 29), for a particular ansatz and target

assertions.value: The authors state that the state-preparation experiment uses 24 qubits with 1 repetition and 1 layer, and that the time-evolution compilation experiment uses 8 qubits.
quotes: we consider the case with n = 24 qubits, b = 1 repetitions and l = 1 layers
Approximate compilation of time evolution operator on 8 qubits

assertions.value: The authors state that their analytic variance result holds for a particular case and conjecture that it holds for more general ansatz and target states.
quotes: We conjecture that such results will hold for more general Ansatz and target states

papers.title_in_file: QUANTUM SIMULATION & OPTIMIZATION OF WATER DISTRIBUTION NETWORKS
papers.what_it_is: A feasibility study that uses emulated quantum linear solvers (VQLS, HHL, QUBO) and annealing inside a Newton-Raphson water network solver.

assertions.value: The authors report that, on emulators, QNR-VQLS scored better than QNR-HHL and QNR-QUBOLS for simulating water flow and pressure on a 2-loop network.
quotes: In conclusion, QNR-VQLS scored better than QNR-HHL and QNR-QUBOLS on simulating water flow and pressure for the 2-loop network.
assertions.certainty_reason: Emulator results on one small network, Section 3.1 and Conclusion
assertions.reader_inference: The comparison is on one 7-node network with no hardware noise. It says nothing about speed.

assertions.value: The authors report that the HHL-based solver did not reproduce the classical results, with a spread much greater than the 10% tolerance region.
quotes: the results obtained with HHL do not reproduce the results obtained with the classical linear solver
the spread of the HHL values is much greater than the tolerance region of 10%.

assertions.value: The authors state that calculations ran on emulators of gate-based quantum computers and with simulated annealing, on small 2-loop networks of 7 nodes, with hardware noise not modelled.
quotes: Calculations were run on emulators of gate-based quantum computers and using simulated annealing while models were tested on small 2-loop networks of 7 nodes.
Noise sources that characterize current generation quantum computers were not accounted for here.

assertions.value: The authors report that the least-cost-design QUBO could not be solved for any network larger than the 0-loop network, which they attribute to the overhead of translating a high-order polynomial problem to a QUBO.
quotes: it was not possible to solve the problem over a larger network than the 0-loop network
This is likely due to the high overhead incurred by translating a high-order polynomial problem to a QUBO.
assertions.certainty_reason: Reported outcome plus the authors' likely explanation, Conclusion

papers.title_in_file: A PAC-Bayesian approach to generalization for quantum models
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Sections I to IV (introduction, preliminaries, informal statements of Theorems 3, 4, 6 and Corollary 5, numerical experiments, discussion). Methods and Appendices A to E (proofs) were not read.
papers.what_it_is: A theory paper deriving non-uniform PAC-Bayesian generalization bounds for layered quantum channel models, with a small numerical check.

assertions.value: The paper derives PAC-Bayesian generalization bounds for layered quantum models built from general quantum channels; the bounds depend on norms of the learned parameter matrices, and the authors describe them as the first PAC-Bayesian bounds for a broad class of quantum models.
quotes: we derive the first PAC-Bayesian generalization bounds for a broad class of quantum models by analyzing layered circuits composed of general quantum channels
we establish non-uniform bounds that depend on the norms of learned parameter matrices
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorems 3 and 4, Section III (full proofs in appendices, not read)
assertions.reader_inference: The first-of-its-kind claim is the authors' own. The bounds can be vacuous in some regimes (the appendix text mentions exponential factors), which the main text does not stress.

assertions.value: The paper extends the bounds to equivariant quantum models and states that priors on symmetry-constrained subspaces reduce the effective KL penalty and yield provably tighter bounds.
quotes: we extend these results to symmetry-constrained equivariant quantum models
reduces the effective KL penalty and yields provably tighter bounds for equivariant quantum models

assertions.value: The authors report, from 1400 independent training runs, positive Pearson correlations of r = 0.26 for a dynamic PQC and r = 0.46 for a QCNN between the complexity term and the generalization gap.
quotes: In Figure 3, we illustrate the results obtained from 1400 independent training runs for the (a) dynamic PQC and (b) QCNN architectures.
yielding a positive Pearson correlation coefficients of r = 0.26 and r = 0.46 for the dynamic PQC and QCNN architectures, respectively.
assertions.certainty_reason: Proof-of-concept experiment, one task, Section III C
assertions.reader_inference: The correlations are weak to moderate and the task is a single phase-classification problem. The numbers show the bound's complexity term tracks the gap, not that the bound is tight.

assertions.value: The authors describe their numerical experiments as proof-of-concept, classifying ground states of a cluster Hamiltonian into four phases with a training set of 8 samples and a test set of 1000 samples.
quotes: we perform proof-of-concept numerical experiments designed to analyze the correlation between our analytically derived generalization bounds and the true performance of quantum models
we utilize a restricted training set of N = 8 samples
The quantum models are evaluated on a separate, independent test set of 1000 samples.

papers.what_it_is: A short theory proposal for a data re-uploading quantum classifier with binary parameters trained by a quantum maximization algorithm.

assertions.value: The authors state that their quantum search-based training reaches a quadratic speed-up over classical brute-force search for the binary trainable parameters.
quotes: We show that we can reach the quadratic speed-up in optimization trainable parameters compared to classical brute force search.
assertions.certainty_reason: Argued complexity estimate with oracle assumptions, Complexity analysis section
assertions.reader_inference: No simulation or hardware run is reported. The speed-up is against brute force over binary parameters, not against practical classical trainers.

assertions.value: The authors state that the speed-up appears only when 2k < n, where k is the number of training points and n is the number of binary parameters.
quotes: If 2k < n, i.e., the number of training points is smaller than the number of parameters we start to observe the speed-up.

assertions.value: The authors state that the algorithm assumes the amplitude needed to choose the nonlinear function can be computed efficiently on a classical computer for each sampled reference.
quotes: it is possible to efficiently calculate the amplitude classically which is needed for the appropriate choice of Q.

assertions.value: The authors state that the full circuit acts on 2(n + 2k) + 6 qubits, where k is the number of training points.
quotes: The full circuit needed acts on 2(n + 2k) + 6 qubits, where k is the number of the training points.
assertions.reader_inference: The qubit count grows with both the parameter count and the training set size, so the circuit is far beyond current hardware for realistic problems.

papers.title_in_file: Extreme Quantum Cognition Machines for Deliberative Decision Making
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Sections 1 to 3, Section 5 results text, Section 6, Section 8. Section 4 algorithm details, Section 7 spectral analysis and Appendices A and B were not read.
papers.what_it_is: A theory and simulation paper that combines quantum cognition with quantum extreme learning for classifying symbolic linguistic data.

assertions.value: The authors report, in simulation on Italian words versus random strings, a training accuracy of 0.9567 and a test balanced accuracy of 0.9625 with dynamical attention, and a drop to a training accuracy of 0.9367 and a test accuracy of 0.9000 with attention off.
quotes: On the training set (panel (b)), the model achieves Accuracy = 0.9567 and BA = 0.9567
with test balanced accuracy BA = 0.9625
a reduction of the training accuracy to 0.9367 and of the test accuracy to 0.9000
assertions.reader_inference: The task (Italian words against random strings) is easy and the test set is small, so the gap may be noise.

assertions.value: The authors report that on Italian versus English words the consonant-vowel encoding gave a test accuracy of 0.9625, while the data-driven two-bucket encoding gave 0.8250 on the test set.
quotes: On the test set (panel (c)), the performance remains essentially unchanged, with Accuracy = 0.9625 and BA = 0.9625
However, on the test set (panel (f)), the performance decreases to Accuracy = 0.8250 and BA = 0.8250.
assertions.reader_inference: The result shows strong sensitivity to the hand-chosen input encoding.

assertions.value: The authors report that in the nearest-neighbour Ising formulation on Task 2, test accuracy was 97.5% with attention active, and state that the explicit attention modulation does not lead to a statistically significant improvement.
quotes: With attention active, the confusion matrix gives TP = 40, TN = 38, FP = 2, and FN = 0, corresponding to an accuracy of 97.5%
the explicit attention modulation does not lead to a statistically significant improvement
assertions.reader_inference: These are classical simulations of a hardware-compatible model, not hardware runs. No significance test is reported.

assertions.value: The authors state that the study remains at the level of proof-of-principle simulations and that systematic benchmarks on larger datasets are needed to assess practical advantages and limitations.
quotes: Although the present study remains at the level of proof-of-principle simulations
systematic benchmarks on structured image datasets, multimodal sensing problems, and biological sequence corpora will be necessary to assess the practical advantages and limitations of the approach
